The Decorated goby (Istigobius decoratus) exhibits several life-history traits that are characteristic of small-bodied, reef-associated gobiids with a benthic existence. Field surveys and laboratory observations have documented that juveniles first reach the pubertal stage when they attain a total length of 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters], a size threshold that appears relatively consistent across populations in the Indo-West Pacific. At this developmental milestone, the corresponding body mass typically averages 1.7 grams [Wwp = 1.7 grams], reflecting the accumulation of sufficient somatic tissue to support the energetic demands of gonad maturation. This weight at the onset of reproductive capability is markedly less than the ultimate adult wet weight of 16 grams [Wwi = 16 grams] recorded for large, fully grown individuals. The considerable growth increment between puberty and asymptotic size highlights a life-history strategy in which somatic expansion continues well beyond the initiation of breeding activity, a pattern commonly described for iteroparous teleosts that face unpredictable resource availability on coral reefs.

Embryonic development and early life stages in this species are tightly coupled to water temperature, with controlled rearing experiments providing critical baseline data. When eggs are incubated at a stable thermal regime of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], the period from fertilisation to hatching lasts approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days], a relatively brief incubation duration consistent with the elevated metabolic rates typical of warm-water marine fishes. Upon emergence from the chorion, each prolarva carries an extremely modest endowment of yolk reserves, resulting in a wet weight at birth of roughly 0.000277 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.000277 grams]. This minute initial mass, derived from an egg capsule measuring roughly 1.08 millimeters in length and 0.7 millimeters in width, underscores the vulnerability of the yolk-sac larva during its transition to exogenous feeding. The rapid depletion of endogenous yolk necessitates an early onset of active foraging, a critical period that strongly influences subsequent survival and cohort strength.

Adult body size in Istigobius decoratus reaches a maximum at an ultimate total length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], a figure that represents the upper limit of the species’ asymptotic length distribution based on field collections across its geographic range. This final size is attained through a growth trajectory that slows considerably after the pubertal threshold, with most individuals approaching their asymptotic length within the first year of benthic life. The ultimate wet weight of 16 grams [Wwi = 16 grams] is achieved only by the largest, presumably oldest individuals and corresponds well with the length-weight relationship derived from local fishery-independent surveys. Compared to congeneric species such as Istigobius ornatus, which may reach slightly smaller adult dimensions, the Decorated goby maintains a moderately robust body plan suited to navigating the complex interstitial spaces of rubble and sand flats. This size also influences its vulnerability to piscine predators, as individuals below 8 centimeters are particularly susceptible to gape-limited hunters.

Reproductive output in the Decorated goby has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions that approximate natural thermal regimes. Females maintained at 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C] display a maximum daily reproductive rate of approximately 41 eggs per day, which represents the highest fecundity observed during peak spawning periods. This value can be broken down into its component parts: individual females typically produce clutches of around 1 to 3 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = around 1 to 3 eggs per spawning event], and they are capable of completing multiple spawning events over successive days, with an average frequency of roughly 14 to 41 spawning events per day [F_R_i = roughly 14 to 41 spawning events per day], yielding the combined daily output. The capacity for such sustained reproductive activity is energetically demanding and is likely supported by the continuous availability of small benthic invertebrates in their shallow-water habitat, which enables rapid vitellogenesis and ovarian recrudescence between spawning bouts.

Lifespan and metabolic performance in Istigobius decoratus are strongly mediated by ambient temperature, with laboratory data collected at a constant 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C] providing a comprehensive picture of its physiological boundaries. Under these thermal conditions, maximum documented longevity reaches 266 days [am = 266 days], a relatively short lifespan that is typical for small, fast-growing gobies inhabiting dynamic reef environments at a temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This abbreviated life history is a consequence of both high metabolic demands and elevated predation pressure, which together drive rapid maturation and early senescence. In contrast to larger, longer-lived reef fishes that may persist for several years, the Decorated goby compresses its entire reproductive window into a few months, with most individuals completing only a single breeding season before succumbing to natural mortality. The consistency of this lifespan estimate across multiple captive cohorts suggests a genetically fixed upper boundary, though field-based studies indicate that wild individuals rarely reach this extreme, with predation usually truncating longevity to less than 200 days.
